newsitem.title: USA: Senate agrees to specific aid amount for Egypt.
newsitem.headline: Senate agrees to specific aid amount for Egypt.

text.p: The Senate on Wednesday agreed to set aside $2.1 billion for military and economic assistance to Egypt after a key senator said he was satisfied Cairo had resumed its leading role in bringing peace to the Middle East.

"It is my hope that the Egyptians are back on track and willing to resume being a constructive partner in the Middle East peace process. Clearly, that is the key to continued U.S. assistance to Egypt," Sen. Mitch McConnell, a Kentucky Republican, said as the Senate debated U.S. foreign aid for the coming year.
The earmark of aid to Egypt was approved on a voice vote as an amendment to the $13.2 billion foreign aid appropriation for fiscal 1998, which starts Oct. 1.

As chairman of the influential Senate Appropriations subcommittee on foreign operations, McConnell cited "emerging ties" with Libya in his refusal last month to earmark aid for Egypt in the 1998 foreign aid legislation.

In announcing his decision to reverse his position, McConnell told the Senate, "I am satisfied, as I am sure the Israeli leadership is, that Cairo has resumed the crucial role we know it has and can play to stabilise the region and secure a durable peace."

Even without his agreement, the Senate's refusal to earmark the aid would have been unlikely to result in a cutoff of funds as it ran counter the Clinton administration's policy. The State Department would have been free to continue the aid from the overall U.S. foreign aid budget.
Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak has assigned a key aide as an intermediary between Israelis and Palestinians and has taken other steps to keep the two sides talking.

Since Egypt and Israel signed the U.S.-brokered Camp David peace accords of 1978 both have been assured a specified share in the annual U.S. foreign aid budget for military and economic assistance. Israel will receive $3 billion in 1998.
